name: 3U CubeSat frame
description: A metal frame the size of a loaf of bread: three 10 cm cubes in a row. Every other part bolts into it.
why_it_matters: The frame sets how much room you have. A small frame is light and cheap to launch, but it fills up fast.
size_source: CubeSat Design Specification Rev 14.1 (Cal Poly, 2022), as tabulated at https://cubesat-specs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_modules/cubesat_specs/form_factors.html
notes: body_size_mm and max_mass_kg are the CubeSat standard's limits for a whole 3U spacecraft, not figures for this frame alone. They were read from a table of the standard, not from the standard's own PDF.

name: 6U CubeSat frame
description: A frame twice the size of the 3U: six 10 cm cubes, two rows of three.
why_it_matters: More room for a bigger camera, battery and radio. The frame is heavier, and bigger parts add more mass and cost.
size_source: CubeSat Design Specification Rev 14.1 (Cal Poly, 2022), as tabulated at https://cubesat-specs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_modules/cubesat_specs/form_factors.html
notes: body_size_mm and max_mass_kg are the CubeSat standard's limits for a whole 6U spacecraft, not figures for this frame alone. They were read from a table of the standard, not from the standard's own PDF.

name: 3U body solar panel
description: A panel of 7 solar cells fixed to one long side of a 3U frame. It makes up to 8.4 W in sunlight.
why_it_matters: Fixed panels are simple and have nothing to unfold. They only make full power when their side faces the Sun.

name: 3U fold-out solar array
description: A double panel of 21 solar cells that unfolds from a 3U frame after launch. It makes up to 25.2 W in sunlight.
why_it_matters: Unfolding panels give three times the power of a fixed one. They add mass and cost, and they must unfold correctly in space.
estimate_basis: The source lists a single (14 cells, 16.8 W) and a double (21 cells, 25.2 W) version, with mass 285 to 468 g and price US$21,000 to 23,400 as ranges. We assume the top of each range belongs to the double version. deployed_area_m2 is not published: 21 cells at the area of the 7-cell 3U panel (one 100 x 340.5 mm face holds 7 cells), with every cell counted as unfolded.

name: 6U fold-out solar array
description: A large array of 32 solar cells that unfolds from a 6U frame. It makes up to 38.4 W in sunlight.
why_it_matters: A power-hungry radio or thruster needs a big array. This one is the heaviest and most expensive power source here.
estimate_basis: The source gives the mass as a range, 655 to 1,065 g, across versions. The top of the range is used. deployed_area_m2 is not published: 32 cells at the area of the 7-cell 3U panel (one 100 x 340.5 mm face holds 7 cells), with every cell counted as unfolded.

name: 36 Wh battery and power unit
description: A battery pack that stores 36 watt-hours, with the electronics that charge it and share power between the parts.
why_it_matters: On every orbit the spacecraft passes through Earth's shadow, where solar panels make nothing. The battery must carry it through.
estimate_basis: The list price is 7,000 GBP (page last updated 22 July 2021). Converted to US dollars at 1.3227 USD per GBP, the European Central Bank reference rate for 13 Nov 2026 (api.frankfurter.dev).

name: 99 Wh battery and power unit
description: A large battery pack that stores 99 watt-hours, made for 6U and bigger frames.
why_it_matters: A bigger battery runs more equipment through the shadow and is drained less deeply, so it lasts longer. It weighs three times as much as the small one.
estimate_basis: Cost: no public price. Scaled by stored energy from the OrbAstro 36 Wh unit (7,000 GBP x 99/36 = 19,250 GBP), then converted at 1.3227 USD per GBP (European Central Bank reference rate, 13 Nov 2026).

name: UHF radio
description: A simple two-way radio for commands and health reports. It sends at most 19.6 kilobits per second.
why_it_matters: Cheap and reliable for talking to the spacecraft. It is far too slow to send pictures home.
estimate_basis: The radio is paired with its maker's matching antenna. The antenna's price is not public and is not counted in cost_musd. antenna_gain_dbi is the published lower bound (more than 0 dBi).
notes: frequency_mhz is the centre of the 435-438 MHz band. rf_power_w is 33 dBm (2 W). power_w is the DC draw while transmitting at 33 dBm.

name: S-band radio
description: A two-way radio on a higher frequency. It sends up to 125 kilobits per second.
why_it_matters: About six times faster than the UHF radio, for twice the power. Still slow for a camera that makes megabits every second.
estimate_basis: The radio is paired with its maker's matching antenna. The antenna's price is not public and is not counted in cost_musd.
notes: frequency_mhz is the centre of the 2200-2290 MHz downlink band. rf_power_w is 33 dBm (2 W). power_w is the maximum DC draw while transmitting; standby_power_w is the receive draw.

name: X-band transmitter
description: A fast one-way radio for sending pictures to the ground. It sends up to 150 megabits per second.
why_it_matters: More than a thousand times faster than the S-band radio, so pictures get home. It draws 18 W while sending and it cannot receive commands.
estimate_basis: The radio is paired with its maker's matching antenna. The antenna's price is not public and is not counted in cost_musd. antenna_gain_dbi is the published lower bound (more than 16 dBi).
notes: Mass is the manufacturer's 396 g (+/- 5%); satsearch lists 270 g. frequency_mhz is the centre of the 8025-8400 MHz band. rf_power_w is the 2 W maximum; power_w is the DC draw at that setting.

name: Onboard computer
description: The spacecraft's brain. It runs the other parts, follows commands from the ground and stores data on two 16 GB memory chips.
why_it_matters: The spacecraft is out of contact for most of each orbit, so the computer must run the mission by itself.
estimate_basis: Power draw is not published (the maker says only "low power consumption"). 0.5 W is a placeholder set by the game team and needs a sourced value.

name: Magnetic pointing unit
description: Electromagnets that push against Earth's magnetic field to turn the spacecraft. It holds a direction to within about 5 degrees.
why_it_matters: A camera has to point at the ground. Magnets are light and cheap, but their aim is rough and they turn the spacecraft slowly.
estimate_basis: The source gives ranges across versions: mass 127 to 207 g, price US$6,000 to 9,000, power below 1 W. The top of each range is used.

name: Precision pointing unit
description: Three spinning wheels and three electromagnets turn the spacecraft, and a star camera tells it exactly which way it faces.
why_it_matters: A sharp camera needs steady, exact aim. This unit gives it, for more mass and much more money than magnets alone.
estimate_basis: Cost: no public price. US$100,000 is a placeholder: three reaction wheels at about the public price of one comparable wheel (Space Inventor WHL-100, 25,000 EUR, satsearch.co) plus a star tracker, rounded. Power is the top of the published 0.94 to 1.4 W range.

name: Electric thruster
description: A thruster that uses electricity to shoot out charged metal atoms very fast. The push is tiny, about a third of a millinewton, but it uses very little propellant.
why_it_matters: A thruster can lift the orbit back up when air drag pulls it down, so the mission lasts longer. This one needs 40 W while firing, more than a small spacecraft may have.
estimate_basis: Cost: no public price and no public comparison; US$50,000 is a placeholder set by the game team. Specific impulse is published as a range, 2,000 to 6,000 s; the lower bound is used. Total impulse is the published minimum (more than 5,000 N s).
notes: mass_kg is the wet mass (680 g dry plus 220 g of indium propellant). thrust_mn is the nominal 330 micronewtons.
